issues.legal_issue: A decree declaring title to property is not a decree for property within the provision requiring court fees based on the value of the property.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declarations of ownership over properties and sought to have an earlier decree declaring another person the owner adjudged void.
The earlier decree declared title but did not order the recovery of money or property.
The plaintiff claimed declaratory relief, and the dispute concerned the court fee payable on the plaint.
issues.conclusion: The provision concerning cancellation of or adjudging void a decree for money or other property did not apply because the challenged decree declared title rather than ordering recovery of property; the court fee paid was proper.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(iv-A) of the Court-Fees Act, as amended by the U.P. Legislature, applies to a decree for recovery of money or other property, not to a decree merely concerning title to property. The Court read “for” consistently with its use in the other clauses of Section 7, where it denotes obtaining a decree ordering payment or recovery. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: court_fee_classification_dispute and declaratory_title_suit and relief_seeks_voiding_prior_decree and prior_decree_declares_title_only

predicates.court_fee_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns the court fee payable on a plaint.
predicates.declaratory_title_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.relief_seeks_voiding_prior_decree: The plaintiff sought to have an earlier decree adjudged void or voidable.
predicates.prior_decree_declares_title_only: The earlier decree declared a person's title to property without ordering its recovery.

issues.definition: When a court-fee classification dispute arises in a declaratory title suit seeking to void an earlier decree that declares title only, the property-recovery decree fee provision does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A decree made in an opposed proceeding is not an instrument securing money or property merely because it records an adjudication concerning rights to property.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to have an earlier decree adjudged void or voidable.
The earlier decree was an adjudication made by the court in an opposed proceeding, rather than a record of a contract between the parties.
The dispute concerned whether the decree fell within the instrument limb of the court-fee provision.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decree was not an instrument securing money or property, and the instrument limb of the provision did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(iv-A) of the Court-Fees Act, as amended by the U.P. Legislature, addresses an instrument securing money or property. A decree made in an opposed proceeding records the court's formal adjudication and does not by its own force secure money or property. A consent decree may be treated as such an instrument where it records a contract that has that effect. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.court_fee_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns the court fee payable on a plaint.
predicates.relief_challenges_property_related_decre: The plaintiff sought to have a decree concerning rights to property adjudged void or voidable.
predicates.prior_decree_is_involuntary: The decree was made by the court in an opposed proceeding rather than by recording a contract between the parties.

issues.definition: When a court-fee classification dispute involves a challenge to a property-related decree made in an opposed proceeding, that decree is not a property-securing instrument.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for a declaration of title is not a subterfuge to avoid property-based court fees when the property is held by another and the declaration would enable recognition of the claimant's rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title to the disputed properties.
The District Magistrate was in possession of the properties.
A declaration of the plaintiff's title would enable the plaintiff to seek recognition of his rights.
The State contended that the declaratory relief was a device to conceal the true nature of the claim.
issues.conclusion: The declaratory relief was not a subterfuge, and the court fee paid on the plaint was proper.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the substance and practical effect of the declaratory relief: because another party held the property, a declaration of title would enable recognition of the claimant's rights. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: court_fee_classification_dispute and declaratory_title_suit and property_held_by_another and declaration_enables_recognition_of_rights

predicates.court_fee_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns the court fee payable on a plaint.
predicates.declaratory_title_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.property_held_by_another: A person other than the plaintiff was in possession of the disputed property.
predicates.declaration_enables_recognition_of_right: A declaration of title would enable the plaintiff to seek recognition of the claimed rights.

issues.definition: When a court-fee dispute concerns a declaratory title suit and another holds the property, a declaration enabling recognition of the claimant's rights means the claim is not a subterfuge.
